So that was the area within which the conversation was to have been conducted and information gathered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And at some point, Mr. Londrovic came back to you informing you that he had, in fact, met with Mr. Petrovic; he had questioned him. And based on that conversation, he had learned from Mr. Petrovic that he could not be of assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not like that, Mr. Karnavas. It wasn't like that. My lawyers in that period of time consulted and spoke to at least 100 potential witnesses, or people that could provide information to them. They passed on to me that they had spoken to Mile Petrovic, that they have their own opinion about all that, and that in the ensuing period contacts would be made with Mile Petrovic and innumerable other people so that they didn't tell me anything specific linked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it was after you learned from Mr. Londrovic that Mile Petrovic could not give assistance to you, that you told Prosecutor the incident with respect to the six prisoners. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, as regards that incident, I told my lawyers this immediately when we started working, and my lawyers knew about it. As for the Prosecutor, I recounted that incident to him when we spoke about it; that is, when we discussed the events along that route on a particular date and in the specific area of Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me make sure I have it right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas is asking leading questions, assuming facts which have been not been placed into evidence, speculating on things that he may or may not have information about that have to do with this person talking with his lawyer. I don't understand the relevance or the propriety of this. Is this some kind of -- it just...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the last paragraph of this document in our hands stated something which is -- which might relate -- might be related to the questions Mr. Karnavas asked. You may proceed along this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me make sure I have it right. You informed your lawyers, Mr. Londrovic and Mr. Kirsch, of this incident early on -- in your working relationship with respect to Mr. Petrovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then you send your lawyers to see whether this person, Mr. Petrovic, could provide you with assistance in your case and give a statement to the effect that -- as to who was giving him orders as a military police officer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, don't ask me in that way because I really can't remember what exactly I said to Mr. Londrovic, Mr. Kirsch, and the investigators. All I can confirm is that one of the persons that needed to be contacted was Mile Petrovic. And of course, with respect to questions related to the military police of which he was a member. And I can't tell you exactly what we talked about, but that was the idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So early on, you gave your lawyers one of the potential witnesses, their names that they should contact, one of them was Mile Petrovic. That's what you're trying to state, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- we hadn't yet defined who the witnesses would be. We were reviewing the situation. We consulted a large number of people, went towards them, spoke to people. But we hadn't yet decided who would be a witness and who would not. And we couldn't anyway because we didn't have anything concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your lawyers came back after meeting with Mr. Petrovic and said -- and told you that he could not help you. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't tell me that he couldn't help me. They conveyed to me roughly what they had discussed with Mile Petrovic. But at the time, we were not deciding whether he could be of assistance to me or not. They simply briefed me on what they had talked about with Mile Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And from what they conveyed to you, it became obvious, Mr. Nikolic, that what the gentleman had to offer as far as information was not helpful to your case. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as a whole. There were parts that my lawyers spoke about and that could be of assistance to me. And there were some things that were not to my benefit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And after that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, I still don't see the relevance of any of this. We could go through this forever in his defence, and we could examine his entire defence and all his relationships with his lawyers. But where does it get us? There's a rule that requires him to put his case to the witness, and I would like to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to respond to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We're not going to debate on that, because I have already made a ruling before that the case lies in the last paragraph of this document. The counsel has the right to know the motive of Mr. Nikolic to state something happened which is different in the counsel's case. It is quite clear. We believe that this issue is relevant. So we allowed Mr. Karnavas to proceed. But I believe somehow you have already got your point. There's no need to pursue it further on this subject. You could not agree the witness totally agreed with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me ask a few more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: After Mr. Londrovic came back and spoke with you about Mr. Petrovic, it was only after that that you went to the Prosecutor and told him of this incident with the six soldiers. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told the Prosecutor about this incident when we -- when the question came up. I really can't say when I mentioned it first. But what I can say is that I said what I said in my statement when I made the statement and when I was talking about that particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic, on that. I have a couple of other matters. Just briefly about the security situation in Bratunac --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we perhaps -- actually, I see here that there was another statement that was given to another organ, the police station in Bratunac this time. And since I have a feeling about this statement, that it was directed and taken for a specific purpose, I would like to ask the Court's indulgence to give us the opportunity to take a look at this second statement as well. Perhaps it could help us clarify certain points, and I express doubts -- I have my doubts here because I see quite a few material mistakes. One of the incorrections by Mr. Mile Petrovic, that he was just an ordinary soldier, for example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it all depends how the counsel will lead you. If he's going to use this document, he'll ask you some questions. If he does not, we could not go into this piece of the evidence. I'm sorry for that. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk -- I just want to focus you back on the security situation in the town of Bratunac on July 13th, just very briefly. Now, according to your testimony, on that particular night, the situation was rather tense this town because of all of the prisoners. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, and I spoke about the -- I did speak about the difficult situation in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe you were asked which units were guarding the buses, and you indicated that you were unable to confirm which units because you never went there to check them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that I did not know all the units or the names of the units from which these members came that provided security for all those buses and the ones that were in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you also said, and I quote from page 1755. This is dated Tuesday, 23 September 2003. I'm quoting from line 11 -- well, let me quote from line 8, the question: "Were there any special police units, the people you have described under the command of Dusko Jevic and Mr. Borovcanin? Were any of those units guarding prisoners in Bratunac this evening?" Referring to the 13th. Your answer was: "I really am unable to confirm which exact units were guarding the prisoners because that evening I wasn't there and I don't know." Do you recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said I wasn't there personally, so I don't know which specific units were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In other words, you never went to check to see who was guarding them, to ask, "Which unit are you from?" Or perhaps recognise some people. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that evening I was engaged on other tasks, and I did not go, no, to see all that there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it was after that time, sometime around 12.30 or so, is when you go to the operation room at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters where you see several officers, including Commander Blagojevic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that evening, that is what I said, that all of them were present because the situation was serious. Bratunac was under threat, and I knew about that individual, so I went to the operational room where I found almost all the officers from the Bratunac Brigade or Bratunac headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, according to your testimony, during the meeting that you had with Deronjic and company, at one point the discussion was whether to engage the entire police force of the RS. That's on page 1752, lines 7 to 11; 753, lines 3 to 7, for the record. Do you recall stating that, there there were some discussions whether to engage the entire RS police force because of how tense the situation was, how insecure Bratunac was at that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember, Mr. Karnavas, is this: That I said that that matter was discussed at the meeting. And I said that as far as I remember, that on that particular evening, a request was made to engage all available forces, perhaps I said police forces, I'm not sure. But if I didn't say that, then all available forces should be engaged in order to provide security for the convoy, the trucks, the prisoners, and everybody who found themselves in Bratunac at that time. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And if I could read back the record, 1752, line 7: "And one of the questions discussed was that that evening, all of the -- the entire police force of the MUP of Republika Srpska should be engaged as well as free soldiers who were free, the military police. And in view of that very serious situation, that volunteers should be called in to assist in the security; that is, all the manpower available should be used to secure the Muslims who were in buses, trucks, in front of the schools, and on sides of the roads, anyway, in the very centre of town." That was your testimony. Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that. That means that that evening, based on the situation that prevailed, that the priority task was to ensure secure conditions in Bratunac. And of course, that all the forces, both police forces and those of the military police and the volunteers and all those bearing weapons should be called in order to provide security for the town, security for the buses and trucks that were scattered round the town in the side streets, on the plateaus, and so on. That's what I said then, and that's what I say now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And then you went to the -- as we said, you went to the operations room around 12.30 or so that evening. You discussed the situation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. The operations room was full. Everybody was there. And the situation and the state of affairs in town at the time was the subject of discussion, what was going in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And that's when you stated that you had this conversation with Colonel Blagojevic, pulling him aside to inform him of your trip to Zvornik. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. That is when I informed first of all those present in the room as to what was happening in Bratunac. And now I can also claim that they all knew what was going on, and I can confirm that on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will answer your question straight away. I will answer your question, yes, yes. Yes, I will, and I apologise. So then I informed Mr. Blagojevic about my trip to Zvornik and the intentions, what was to happen to those people, the prisoners that were in Bratunac at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that was when it was, you know, just four eyes, you and him, and four ears, just your ears and Colonel Blagojevic's ears. Right? That kind of conversation, nobody else heard that take place.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing special except what was heard in the operations room, what we discussed. I didn't convey anything else to him. So apart from what the others heard, I just told him that I had been in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My question is when you pulled him aside and had the conversation about Zvornik, is it not a fact that that was -- that conversation could only be heard, if this conversation took place, by him. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that. You could put it that way, that we talked tete-a-tete, or in four eyes, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's the expression I believe that's used in Bosnia, so that's why I thought I'd use it. After that, according to your testimony, and I have it here in the transcript, page 1759, you indicated that you went to the MP building, the military police building, to see if there were any military police available, to engage them. But you had no luck. There weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what I remember is that at the military police, there was just the police officer on duty. And that there weren't any more policemen there who could have been engaged on that assignment. They were elsewhere on assignment that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe it was after that point that you were asked, 1759, line 21, "then what did you do?" And your answer was: "Nothing. It was late, and I went to sleep after that." That's your testimony. You did nothing. You went back to sleep. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. I said that after that, I did nothing, and that after that, I went off to sleep. And I can just add one more sentence there, that means that what I knew at that point in time was that the people who were in the school were secure. And as to the other -- further responsibilities, that was up to the logistics organs to take care of the prisoners. And so as I had no means of seeing to that, and actually didn't come under my competence either, I did nothing. I took no steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So let me sum it up: Everybody thinks in that meeting that this is a dangerous situation for the town of Bratunac, not for the prisoners but for the town of Bratunac. There's a discussion with respect to mobilising all available police -- the police force and volunteers. You don't know who's guarding them. You have this supposed conversation at the operations room. And then the situation, which remained volatile, nonetheless, you went home to your family in Bratunac and went to sleep. That's the point I'm trying to make. Is that correct? Is that the sequencing of it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karnavas. You just now said something that I did not, in fact, say, and that is the observation that I did not know who was providing security for all those prisoners. I separated that. I did know who was securing the prisoners in the facilities, in the schools and the hangar, the gym hall, and the secondary school centre. But I did not know who was providing security for the captured who -- during the night, who were there during the night when I wasn't there, when I was in Zvornik. That means that a vast number of buses arrived. I can't say 80, 100, 120 buses and trucks. I don't know the exact number, but a lot of them. And they were scattered throughout town, parked all over town, so I don't know who secured them then. How this was done. Which units there were. Whether there was enough or not. I know nothing about that. And that's what I'm saying, that's what I'm testifying about. I'm saying I don't know which people provided security for those buses and trucks that turned up during the night. And that's the truth of it. That's what I'm claiming, and that's what I said in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Okay. But the situation still remained volatile when you went to sleep. The town of Bratunac was still insecure when you went to sleep, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, the security of the town was not just my job. The security of the town, the town itself, the town proper, was more up to the police forces to secure because during that period of time, everything was functioning. The civilian authorities, police authorities, and everything else. So it wasn't me. I wasn't the one alone who was responsible for the town of Bratunac. There were a series of other structures who were responsible for it, too. And among other things, I had my role in all this, amongst all these others, and I think I did what I could. And I had to go to bed, to go to sleep because I had stayed up until 3.30 a.m. the previous night. So I couldn't take it any more, and I had to get some sleep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We didn't get your point, frankly speaking, but move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Every time you've communicated with Colonel Blagojevic, on the 12th, on the 13th and so on, up until the 17th, it would appear that the communications were four eyes and four ears only. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, during that period of time, every time I wished to communicate with the commander or with any other commanding officer, the only way was to communicate that way, to communicate personally and to report to him. During that time, there was no reporting. There were no meetings. So the only way in which I could communicate with the commander was that way, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there's no one to verify whether indeed you did make any communications with him. And if so, what exactly you communicated. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said. In these cases, I communicated personally with Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And there's no one to verify what, if anything, was said on the morning of the 12th between you, Kosoric, and Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I have explained the situation that we were in. I said who was present, and you can draw your own conclusions. But I said how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And nobody is available to verify whether, indeed, you were ordered by Colonel Jankovic to do anything on July 12th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that, too. And I have nothing further to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Let's move on to another topic. Yesterday we talked a little bit about the negotiating process. And we were discussing, and at one point you indicated, and I quote -- I believe it's page 67 on the transcript from yesterday's, and I'm reading sort of the unofficial version of it. But it starts with page 67, and it's 23:54:17 [sic]. "That's where -- and all of these circumstances created an impression in my mind that there could be some misunderstanding. To be quite frank, I was convinced that most of what I had been saying to the Prosecution, that the Prosecution already has the facts and circumstances about all of that, and all these were factors that prompted me to come to the conclusion that all this may not be sufficient for an agreement. It was along those lines that my thoughts were at the time." Do you recall making that statement, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. I think that in the context of what you asked me, that I tried to explain to you my guiding thoughts and my line of thinking at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And from looking at all of the discovery and discussing it with your lawyers, you knew that the Prosecution had no such information about a meeting where you were tasked or informed by Popovic and Kosoric on the 12th. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not following you, Mr. Karnavas. What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question is by this point, you had spent a lot of time reading all of these documents and discussing these documents with your lawyers. And you knew from reading everything and discussing them with your lawyers that in those documents, there was nothing about you or anyone else being informed on the morning of the 12th of a plan to execute the separated men. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those documents, if you mean the Prosecution documents, the ones I got from the Prosecution, then in those documents I did not find any explicit sentence which would claim that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there was nothing explicit or implicit that Colonel Jankovic had tasked Captain Nikolic to coordinate units in Potocari the morning of July 12th, 1995. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, at that period of time, I did not have all the documents which the Prosecution had at its disposal. What I did have -- in the ones I did have, I did not see that, what you're talking about. I didn't see that in the documents that I had. However, and I do apologise, however, on the basis of an analysis of my indictment, that is to say, what was set out in my indictment, I was going through a process of thought in which, quite simply, I was looking to find myself, see where I was in all that, knowing what I did and what I worked on and what I took part in. So quite simply, I had an idea of my own participation in everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, or at least how the Prosecution saw it, saw your participation.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I could do was to see on the basis of the indictment how the Prosecution sees my participation and to assess that. And I couldn't do that on the basis of any other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And based on all the documents that you had, nothing explicit or implicit that would give you or anyone else the impression that there was an order by Colonel Jankovic to you on that morning when you had that meeting outside the Hotel Fontana. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing like that was written. But there were a series of -- there was a series of information, a series of events and incidents of which I had both a recording and everything else. So of course it wasn't set out in detail in those documents and in my indictment. Not all the details were introduced there. But there was a series of meetings, events. Quite simply, there were those things during that period of time on the basis of which, on the grounds of which I was able to draw certain conclusions myself and to see myself there in what was going on. That's the only way I can explain this to you. So no, it did not state that in a single sentence, no. But the events were recorded. The people were there. I knew about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. You saw yourself on video outside the Hotel Fontana with Kosoric and Popovic. Right? You were there. So at least we have a photograph of you, and that's one of the facts that you saw that was in the hands, in the possessions of the Prosecution. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karnavas. I knew of my meeting with Kosoric and Popovic. I knew of my meeting with Jankovic. I knew about everything they conveyed to me, and I knew about all the other contacts I had with the commanding officers before the Prosecution ever supplied me with any videotapes. I knew all this. Of course, the videotapes were confirmation of what I already knew before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, did you see yourself on the video at that Hotel Fontana with Kosoric and Popovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I did see myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in the documents that you had received and you went over with your own lawyers, there was nothing there implicit or explicit that would show that you had these communications with Colonel Blagojevic, the ones that you claim to have had now, now that you claim that you had between the two of you. There's nothing in there.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In concrete terms, the way you are saying, I did not find anything, or rather I didn't remember anything. If you mean in the documents supplied by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we don't have any videoclips --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you want to finish?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said that I don't remember the details from the indictment now, whether any mention was made about that. As to the meetings, I think there are a series of documents. If you're asking me about those documents, then there are a series of documents testifying to the meetings in the Bratunac Brigade during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So we have some documents that there were some meetings. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're asking me about documents. And I'm saying that I saw documents which said that there were meetings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in none of those documents where those meetings took place, regarding those meetings, show that Colonel Blagojevic was in those meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that's a misstatement of the facts. One of the documents has him right there leading the meeting where certain things were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm talking -- let me rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yeah, maybe you could rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm talking about the 11th -- you didn't see him on the 11th. But the 12th, the 13th, the 14th, the 15th, the 16th, there are no documents that you have seen with respect to meetings - not talking about activities; I'm talking about meetings - that has Colonel Blagojevic in there along with the big players, Mladic, Krstic, or any of the others.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, your question is not quite clear to me. I know that there are no documents of the Bratunac Brigade which state that Mr. Blagojevic participated together with the big leaders, as you call them, at these meetings. But I also know that in the documents disclosed by the Prosecution, there is evidence that all those meetings, or rather the meetings mentioned were held in the command, in the headquarters, of the Bratunac Brigade. There are -- there's an intercept in which it says that Commander Blagojevic is at a meeting upstairs with those from above. So that is what I can say and what I can recall just now, because I have gone through a large number of documents. And that particular document, as far as I can recollect, that intercept I think relates to the 12th. I'm not sure about that, or the 13th maybe. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're not a participant in that intercept, are you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, my name is mentioned in that intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you involved directly in the intercept? Are you on that intercept making that claim, assuming that it is what you claim it is?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a direct participant in the conversation. But my name is mentioned in that intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's -- that intercept is during the period when you went home to get some rest when you were supposed to be on duty. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. It was the period of time when I was on duty and I had completed my duty about 3.00 a.m. And in accordance with the rules of service, my deputy replaced me midnight, much later than he should have replaced me in fact, Mirko Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you were actually covering for him; he wasn't covering for you? Never mind. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't covering for him. The duty service consists of two officers. One is the duty officer, and the other one his deputy. One of the them is on duty one part of the day, and the other one for the other part of the day. And he was my deputy on duty in the operations room, in the operations duty service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. In any event, during the negotiations when you were talking to Mr. McCloskey and his team and giving him all of this information, the truth as you knew it back then, at some point you came to the conclusion that you just weren't giving them enough facts to convince him that he should give you up to a 20-year sentence rather than the life sentence that is probably more appropriate for your conduct. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, that is your assessment. I testified about that yesterday, and I said everything I have to say about that. And I really have nothing more to add to what I said then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one last housekeeping matter. Trisic, you know the gentleman, don't you? He was the assistant commander for rear services?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Major Dragoslav Trisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before you got arrested, you were aware, were you not, that Mr. Trisic had met with the Prosecution at least on one or two occasions to give statements?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Trisic met and how many times. I do know that he once told me that he had an invitation for a conversation. You can check that out. I never spoke to Trisic either before his interview, and after that, he never conveyed to me what happened during that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But my question was - maybe I didn't phrase it correctly - before being arrested, you knew that he had been interviewed by the Office of the Prosecution. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say that I knew that they talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you give us an explanation as to why you had your lawyer put his name with the Registrar to be your investigator on this case in which you knew he was a witness or a potential witness for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know, Mr. Karnavas, that he was a witness or a potential witness or anything like that. I didn't know at all. And to be quite frank, I didn't know anything about the legal provision that somebody that the Prosecution has interviewed could not be an investigator. I was not aware of that. And the decision to engage him as an investigator, my decision, was prompted by the fact that Dragoslav Trisic was for many years commander of the TO staff, and then chief of staff. He was in the army for a long time. He is familiar with the situation in Bratunac. He knows many people. And those were the reasons for my decision. As for this other thing, I really didn't know. And when we learned about that, we gave up the idea and engage somebody who could do that. And that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct. Your lawyer learned it from me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was a sleazy backstab at lawyers. Perhaps you missed that, Your Honour, but that was an attack on these counsels' integrity and it's completely unnecessary. I know nothing about the situation. I wish we could strike that until we get down to the bottom of what the devil he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, this was not an attack on the lawyers. The lawyers were early in the case. They were not expected to know what is contained in the disclosure material. This witness, however, did know because Bratunac is a small town. And I maintained that he wanted somebody on the inside trying to influence witnesses. That's the point. And if the Prosecutor doesn't get it, he can ask me, and I can tell him what the point is. But it's pretty obvious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I believe that you have a point in these questions. The problem is that you have to present it in a proper way. Well, thank you, Mr. Karnavas, for your cross-examination. And I believe that you are ahead of the time. And this afternoon, I think we'll start at 3.00 instead of 3.15, because the reason for doing that is to allow all the people to have a decent lunch, which will probably last 90 minutes. But now we have enough time for that. So we'll resume at 3.00 in the same courtroom. The hearing is adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.12 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, as you indicated that you only need the time of one sitting to cross-examine this witness, I believe that will be 75 minutes, the normal sitting time. I hope we could have 15 minutes after the witness leaves the courtroom to discuss your two motions concerning other procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will respect the time limit. Also, in view of the answers given by the witness today, I hope that we will be able to finish this in less than 75 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed. Yes, Mr. Blagojevic? THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but I would ask your leave to allow me to put a couple of important questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's a very complicated question, I mean procedurally speaking. And we'll consider your request, and this witness will be here tomorrow. And tomorrow morning, I'll give you a reply. THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On behalf of Dragan Jokic and his Defence team, I would like to ask you a few questions, fully aware of the fact that we have nothing in particular to discuss from your statement. During the examination-in-chief by the Prosecutor, you spoke about the duties of the duty officer, and you spoke about that today, too, that is, the time during which you were the officer on duty. I just wanted to ask you whether it is true that the night between the 12th and the 13th of July, you were the duty officer in the Bratunac Brigade of the?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic. In my testimony, I said that I was the duty officer in the command of the Bratunac Brigade on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me according to the instructions for the work of commands and headquarters how is the procedure of the handing over of duty carried out by the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you very briefly. There are two parts of this handing over of duty. A part of it has to do between the duty officer and his assistant, and the second part of the procedure, as far as I know, deals with the handing over of duty between the previous duty officer and the next duty officer in the hall. These are the two parts of this handing over of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about this second type of handing over of duty between the previous duty officer and the coming duty officer. How is it done and in whose presence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is what the practice was and what was done in practice in the Bratunac Brigade. I cannot say how this was regulated in other brigades. What happens is that the previous duty officer who spent certain time on duty familiarises the next duty officer of obligations and tasks if he has any that had been ordered by the superior command, about current duties that again stem from the requirements of subordinate units or orders from superior commands, orders, hypothetically speaking, from the commander or chief of staff of his own unit which may have been issued or need to be passed on. And that would be the customary matters that the duty officer would inform his successor of. There may be other matters, but this is a broad issue, and I don't think it's necessary for me to go into the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is a book signed, a report indicating that duty has been handed over?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it any kind of report or minutes, at least I'm not familiar with it. And we didn't proceed in that way. During the handing over of duty, there is the duty book which -- in which all these matters that I have mentioned are recorded, and then the next duty officer is familiarised with these things. And it was customary for this book to contain all these observations and issues, and it was customary to write at the end "duty handed over by" and then the previous duty officer would sign. And then in the other corner, "duty taken over by," and again, signed by the person taking over duty. And that would be the whole procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And on this report on the handing over of duty, does the commander or chief of staff approve this and confirm this by his signature?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Bratunac Brigade, we didn't have that practice for the commander to sign this. It may have been the practice in some other brigades, but in view of the fact there's a plan of operations duty drafted in the brigade, that plan is usually approved by the commander or chief of staff. So this plan of duty had already been approved, according to my understanding. Therefore, I am not aware of any practice that the commander, and I'm talking about the Bratunac Brigade, would be present when duty was handed over. That was not the practice in the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I infer from that that it was obligatory for the chief of staff or the commander to be present, but that this was not carried out in practice?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot confirm that because I cannot refer to any rule of service specifying that because I'm not sufficiently familiar with that segment. I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this change of duty in the brigade fixed? Was there a fixed time when this was done?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, one duty shift would last, as far as I remember, 24 hours. So duty would be taken over in the morning, and it would be handed over the next day in the morning. Again, I'm not quite certain whether that is the duration, but I think that is how it was. I think you would take over duty one day, and hand it over the next day. As far as I can remember, this would happen in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Judging by what you just told me, your duty should have started on the 12th in the morning and should have ended on the 13th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does the rules of service of the security organ envisage the possibility for the intelligence security officer to be the duty officer in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Stojanovic. Chapter 9, paragraph 93 of the rules of service of the security organ defines this duty service and explicitly stipulates that an officer in the security service cannot be the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In spite of such an explicit rule, you were designated as the duty officer from the 12th to the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in spite of that and in spite of my warnings to all the commanders of the Bratunac Brigade that security organs and police officers should not be planned as duty officers in the brigade, it was the regular practice for me to be the duty officer, before Srebrenica and after Srebrenica and always, regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this something that was established in the Bratunac Brigade in advance as a list of duty officers?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Bratunac Brigade, a plan of duty officers was drafted. I don't remember whether this was done on a seven-day, ten-day, or 15-day basis. But on the basis of such an approved plan of the chief of staff, or the commander - again, I'm not quite sure who approved it - so on the basis of this written plan, duty service was carried out in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question on this subject: Would it happen that in the morning on that same day, a duty officer would be appointed extraordinarily, or was that plan respected regularly?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was on duty, it would happen frequently - I know that this happened to other officers from the senior command - that an officer would replace him who had more time. So such replacements were allowed for a couple of hours, two, three, or five hours, depending on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was such a replacement done with the knowledge of the commander and chief of staff or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, such replacements were known. One of the officers, senior officers, whether he be the chief of staff or the commander, would know about it, and he would not oppose it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that such replacements would not be in order unless the commander or chief of staff were informed about them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, Mr. Stojanovic, whatever is prescribed by the law and the rules should be complied with. So if the commander and the chief of staff do not decide otherwise or do not allow something else to take place, I don't know whether you can make such a conclusion. All I can say is that in the Bratunac Brigade, this was not -- this was never treated as an infringement of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But according to the rules, this should be done with the approval of the commander or chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Whatever is prescribed by the rules should be complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that in every battalion, there would be either an assistant commander or an officer for intelligence and security affairs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In each infantry battalion, there would be an assistant commander for intelligence, security affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So that is the precise title, "assistant commander"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What are the duties of that assistant commander for security and intelligence work in the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many duties, but I shall try and tell you briefly what they are. The duties of the assistant commander for intelligence and security affairs in a battalion is in the area of responsibility of his battalion and in the area -- I'm sorry, I can't find the right word, the right term. In the area of responsibility of the battalion and the intelligence zone of the battalion to gather all information about the activities of the enemy in front of him, to propose to the battalion commander all measures to prevent any infiltration of sabotage and terrorist and other armed groups within the area of responsibility of the battalion, to propose to the commander the most effective and efficient way of using the reconnaissance unit. And in a battalion, there are reconnaissance squads. And to organise, in accordance with the requirements of a superior officer or commander, to organise reconnaissance patrols, scouts, observers, observer posts, and to train all those reconnaissance elements. And whatever is gathered as a result of the work of these reconnaissance elements in the battalion to be placed at the disposal of the commander so that he might have a clear idea of what is to be found ahead of him in his area of responsibility. So that would be in brief the duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said twice "inform his commander." When you say "inform his commander," which commander do you mean? Of the battalion or of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I say this, and we were talking about the battalion, I mean the battalion commander because he was the direct assistant commander in that unit. So he would inform his commander about everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I conclude from this that it is to the assistant commander for intelligence and security in the battalion that the battalion commander is in command of him? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Stojanovic, that's right. The assistant in the battalion has the battalion commander as his commander. And that same assistant down the line vertically is -- has the chief of the intelligence in the brigade above him, and he is duty-bound to inform the assistant commander for intelligence and security about all intelligence in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And if he is duty-bound to do so, then can I conclude that he is responsible for his work to the battalion commander? Is that who he is responsible to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is responsible for his work to the commander of the battalion, and the battalion commander is directly in command of that assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll try in concrete terms to touch upon the counts in the indictment which refer to my defendant. In paragraph 9, tab 1, tab (a) of the statement of facts, you say, and I'm going to paraphrase, that after the execution in Kravica, soon afterwards on the 13th of July, 1995, machines were brought in from Zvornik and Bratunac to bury the bodies. Now, in that context and in that respect, I wish to ask you to clarify a few points. Do you know what machinery this was? What kind of machines were they?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question, or rather when it comes to this kind of information, I said that I learned that the bodies from Kravica, they were -- bodies from Kravica, and people who were killed and lost their lives, that I learned that they were from Zvornik, or rather, that the engineering machinery came from Zvornik, or civil construction machinery came from there, from Zvornik and from Bratunac as well, this construction machinery. I learned about that from the director of the communal services company in Bratunac, Mr. Dragan Mirkovic was his name. And that's what I relayed and conveyed further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And can I ask you how Dragan Mirkovic could know about that? Was it an operation he took part in and so knew about it that way? Did he say anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, Dragan Mirkovic, or rather I talked to him many times about that with him before I was arrested and before I came here. And Dragan Mirkovic told me himself that he had taken part in the operation to bury the Muslims who were killed and lost their lives during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Dragan Mirkovic ever tell you that they were machines from the civilian sector, or whether they were machines from the Zvornik Brigade perhaps? Which? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Dragan Mirkovic did not tell me that they were machines from the Zvornik Brigade ever. Dragan Mirkovic told me that I think that they were dredgers which were yellow in colour. He never said that the machinery was actually from the Zvornik Brigade, excavators yellow in colour. I don't know who they belonged to, either the company or whether they were the property of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just deal with one more dilemma. Can you tell us when that machinery was functioning? On what day, what day was it working?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed the period when they were put to use -- we didn't discuss the period when they were put to use, and I wasn't actually interested in it. I could just make a guess, but I don't want to do so. So during that critical -- we were discussing that critical period of time and the use of that machinery, so I can only make a guess, but I don't want to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the critical period," do you mean that particular day, the 13th, or the next few days, the 14th, for example? What do you mean when you say "the critical period"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I say "critical period," I mean the days, or rather, first of all, the 13th, the 14th, the days when according to Dragan Mirkovic's statement these bodies were buried, if you're asking me about this critical period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So can I take it, then, that that critical period is the 13th and 14th? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I can confirm on the basis of what Mirkovic Dragan said during our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we just clear one more point up. Did anybody say who worked this machinery that was yellow and came from Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he happen to say that it was a soldier or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And one more question in that same context: Did you hear from Dragan Mirkovic perhaps or from anybody else that there were trucks, some trucks that came from Zvornik, too, or were you just referring to the construction machinery?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we just spoke about these construction -- this construction machinery that was brought in on trucks, and they were referred to as "truck trains." But we didn't discuss the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he perhaps say who led this operation in Bratunac, or rather, Kravica, this burial operation? Was it the army? Was it civil defence? Was it a civilian group of people, or perhaps somebody else entirely?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Mirkovic told me that he was personally in charge of clearing, or rather transporting the bodies and digging the graves and the cleansing of the terrain as a member of the civil defence unit in Bratunac at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I take it, then, that it was the civilian protection sector of Bratunac that managed the operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really tell you what conclusion you yourself can make. I'm just telling you what I know and it's up to you. I can't comment on what conclusion you're going to draw from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me put the question a different way, then. Was it the army, the Bratunac Brigade soldiers who were in any shape or form in charge of cleaning up the terrain, or rather dealing with the bodies from Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know and the information that reached me, I don't know that the Bratunac Brigade organ in organised fashion or in any other way took part in the burial process, in burying the corpses from Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And Dragan Mirkovic, who was director of the communal service for Bratunac, was also the commander of the civil defence in Bratunac. Is that right, at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he actually was establishmentwise. All I know is that he belonged to the civil defence or civil protection sector. But what post he held when he was mobilised and anything else, I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, you said at one point, and I'll revert to that statement of facts, the same one, point 2 or paragraph 2, that from the intelligence officer of the 2nd Infantry Battalion, you got information as to what was happening in Potocari on the 11th, or rather, the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, perhaps I misspoke, made a slip of the tongue. If I said from the intelligence security organ, then that would mean that I received it directly. What I meant to say was that I received this intelligence from the 2nd Infantry Battalion, from the intelligence reconnaissance group. I think I made a slip of the tongue on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to read it out to you, and then we can comment. And I'll read it in B/C/S. "I received that information from the intelligence officer of the 2nd infantry battalion."

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite possibly I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But it means you didn't get it from the officer, but from the service. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was the intelligence reconnaissance organs under the brigade command, and perhaps I had misspoken or said something that was too narrow. So let me put it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you can't mention a single name, the name of an officer from whom you received that piece of information from?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state who I got all the information and intelligence from, the man in the 2nd Infantry Battalion. I can give you a name, the name of the officer who was assistant commander for intelligence and security in the 2nd Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you can't tell us that you actually got that information and intelligence from him? You mean you got it from him or from his service?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can confirm -- actually, there was a lot of information and intelligence coming in during that period of time from the 2nd Infantry Battalion. And it would be quite wrong if I were to state that he was the only one who supplied me with information and intelligence because as I say, there was a lot of intelligence coming in during those days from the 2nd Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And who was the officer in the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officer who was assistant commander for intelligence and security affairs was Milenko Jovanovic from the 2nd Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On the 12th and 13th of July, parts of the 2nd and 3rd Infantry Brigade of the Bratunac Brigade were in Potocari during the period of time you said you coordinated the units. Did you happen to see any officers from those units down there at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, I did see officers from the 2nd Infantry Battalion. In point of fact, I saw Zoran Kovacevic, who was the deputy commander of the company or commander of the company. I saw another officer as well who was the leader or commander of the so-called intervention platoon of the 2nd Infantry Battalion, a platoon that doesn't exist in establishment terms, but it did in actual fact. And his name was Zoran Milosavljevic. I saw him. I also saw many other soldiers from that same battalion, or a number of soldiers from the Zoran Milosavljevic unit, some soldiers from another unit belonging to Zoran Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's go back for a moment to the section in your statement when you went up to Zvornik on the 13th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I need remind you of what you said. We're talking about the evening of the 13th, and your arriving at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. You said you had been to see the duty officer in the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade, that you introduced yourself and said what it was all about. Was it the duty officer, and did you go inside the room of the duty officer at the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't put it that way, Mr. Stojanovic. I said that they took me to the office, which was up on the first storey in the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. And quite simply, I gained the impression that it was the duty officer's office. I did not know the offices in the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. I just said that it was most probably this office, that I had most probably gone there. They didn't take me anywhere else. So I assume that that was the office belonging to the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I was wrong when I asked you that because I have the statement in front of me, and you said that you went to the duty officer, that you asked to meet with Drago Nikolic, and in the duty officer's office somebody met me whom I thought was from the intelligence and security sector.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said I went to that room, to that office. And as far as I remember, I said they called this man to come in. When I said that I was looking for Drago Nikolic, I had to wait in the office, and then they brought in a man who asked me whether he could of any assistance with respect to Drago Nikolic, whether he could help me there. And I said to him that I have to convey to Drago Nikolic personally a message and an order, and that's where we concluded our conversation, in that very same office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you help us ask describe the man you talked to if you didn't know him personally?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Zvornik Brigade, apart from Vinko Pandurevic and Drago Nikolic at that period of time, I didn't know anybody else. I can't really tell you anything special, any characteristic features of that man. Quite simply, I didn't pay that much attention. I wasn't that interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, can I ask a specific question: Do you now know Dragan Jokic? Could that man have been Dragan Jokic if you know the man now?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know Dragan Jokic then at the time. I do know who Dragan Jokic is today. And I'm not quite sure. I can't really say whether it was Dragan Jokic or not. I didn't really pay that much attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Jokic wasn't the duty officer on that night, the 13th. But for the Court and for us, we had to clear up that it wasn't Dragan Jokic. But you say it wasn't him, but you don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, even if it were him, it wouldn't have meant anything because I didn't pay any attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that after that, you went on to the forward command post of the Zvornik Brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recollect who you spoke to there and how you reached the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, by car, I mean the forward command post of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reached the forward command post escorted by a soldier from the Zvornik Brigade who was allotted to me to take me there. We went there in one car, in my car.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of a building was it at the forward command post? Could you remember?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, it was nighttime, and all I can say is that it was a road that was rather narrow. It seemed to me to be about 6, 7, or 8 kilometres away. We got there, only just managed to turn the car around where I had to do so. And it was just a house. Whether it was a holiday home or not, I really don't know. I just went inside that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, from the street, you went into the house where you found Drago Nikolic. You said you turned the car around.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I parked the car, got out of the car. And I was taken by the policeman to this -- these premises where the forward command post was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But where did you turn the car around?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We turned the car around. I don't know how many metres forward. We turned the car around, went back, and parked the car facing the direction from which we had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this the yard of that building or was it the street, the road?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I claim that we didn't make a turning into a yard or anywhere else from the road, as far as I can remember these details now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And when you reached the forward command post, you say that you met Drago Nikolic and spent about ten minutes with him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was anyone else there apart from Drago Nikolic attend while you had that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as I can remember we spoke alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of that conversation, did you return alone, or did Drago Nikolic go with you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Drago Nikolic remained at the forward command post, and the policeman and myself went back towards the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is something I wanted to ask you about. Did Drago Nikolic know that you were coming? Did anyone tell him on the phone that you were coming?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot say now whether somebody told Drago Nikolic that I was about to come. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe put it this way: Did you announce to Drago Nikolic that you would be coming to tell him something important?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was given an assignment in the centre of town. And in that period of time, I didn't use a telephone. I didn't drop by anywhere, and I didn't call him from the Zvornik Brigade. Somebody from the Zvornik Brigade may have called him up and told him, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then you left. You got into the car with that same policeman, and you went back. Did you notice whether there were any other buildings and soldiers in those buildings, or was that building all alone, the one you spoke to Drago Nikolic in? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I really didn't pay any attention as to what was to be found along that road or round about there, nor did I have any reason to look around to see what buildings there were. I told you it was dusk or dark already. I was brought there under escort, and I returned with the same policeman after this talk without any intention of making any observations. I didn't pay any attention to the appearances of my surroundings, the road or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question: When you reached the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, not the forward command post but the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade, you said that you first reported to the policeman at the gate, the security officer. You told him who you were and what you were.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was your arrival recorded in any kind of book, your arrival at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters that you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't deny it, but I can't claim that it was either. At the reception, I showed my pass. I had a pass which I had made in the Kartonaza in Bratunac, a pass with my photograph on it, my full name, and my particulars from my ID. And with that pass, as I never had an official ID, I had this pass. I didn't carry my ID with me. And I showed this pass at the entrance when I reached the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. I said I was from the Bratunac Brigade. I said that I was a security organ, and that I needed Drago Nikolic in person. Now, whether anyone noted that down or not, I don't know. But they didn't stop me. I had no problems. They let me pass. They did not disarm me as was customary. So this is what I'm sure of as having happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As you are an intelligence and security officer, and a good one, was it their duty to record the arrival of such a person, that is, an officer from another brigade? Shouldn't that have been noted down somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Stojanovic, what their superior officers' instructions were. I know that in the Bratunac Brigade, security organs and intelligence security organs would announce themselves with me. They would inform me by telephone, and then I would receive those men. And as far as I know, in my brigade, there was no registering of names at the gate of intelligence and security organs. I don't think other senior officers' names were recorded either, if we knew who they were. If we knew their identity and their positions, men from the corps command, from superior, or even subordinate units, that was not the practice. The rules may have required it, but as far as I know, we did not comply with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that this was not the case, you were not announced, your arrival was not announced. The officer for intelligence and security affairs didn't tell the receptionist to let you pass. You arrived unannounced. You introduced yourself, and you were allowed to enter. So it's contrary to what you were just saying.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my omission. I don't know how these things were regulated in that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But let me just finish with this. When you reached the forward command post, was there somebody on duty, somebody securing the post? Did you report your arrival there? Was this registered?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no one there to stop me. The only thing I could hear was the communications that existed. I don't know what kind. But nobody registered me. Nobody searched me or asked for my ID. No, no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned this concept of asanacija or clearing or sanitisation. Can you tell me what it means in the military sense.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term asanacija in the military sense, first of all, it is a measure that is taken within the system of civil defence measures. One of the measures being asanacija. And in the military sense, it means cleaning the battlefield or the terrain after combat operations, removing dead bodies, corpses of animals and various other objects and things that could provoke an epidemic later on. That would be the briefest definition of this concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that this is quite a legal and legitimate military activity?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can agree that it is a legal measure within the scope of civil defence which is resorted to after combat activities and after the -- after casualties, after burning, destruction, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Talking about this reburial of victims, you spoke about that, too. And at one point in time you confirmed that this was an order from the main staff. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. It was conveyed to me by Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic that this was a main staff order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, did he tell you that you were the person who would in the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade be the coordinator of these reburial activities?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic spoke about the operation, the need to move the graves up there, and he told me that I needed to coordinate those activities and organise the operation of reburial, and that I should be engaged as well as the machinery, the fuel, how fuel should be checked. That is, the logistic support was also discussed, to put it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this was a secret activity going from the main staff via the corps to the brigades?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could tell you that at the outset, one could say that this was a clandestine or secret operation. But in view of the course of the operation, the number of participants, the number of vehicles, the logistic support, the number of people involved, in my judgement, in my assessment, it could not have been a secret operation. Possibly there were ambitions to keep it secret, but I'm saying that in view of all that happened, it could not have been a secret operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So we are drawing the conclusion that this was meant to be a secret operation, but because of the large number of participants, the involvement of machinery, it could not be concealed. Is that the right way to put it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you insist again on me qualifying the operation. I would rather not qualify it because I was not given any order that would indicate to me that it was a secret operation. No measures were taken to infer that it was a secret operation. That may have been the intention of the main staff. They may have -- that may have been defined as a secret assignment, but I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But a moment ago, you said that it probably should have been a secret operation. On what basis are you making that conclusion, then?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an intelligence and security organ, I can make conclusions on the basis of what was being done. Do you think that such an operation would be widely publicised? Don't you share my own opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know it was secret, but I'm asking you to answer on what basis you said today that it probably should have been a clandestine operation, and that's a very logical question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we have to cool for a minute. Mr. Stojanovic, you have to understand that you and this witness speak the same language. So please make a pause after you hear the answer from this witness. It is a very bad practice for you and the witness to speak at the same time in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. May I proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Allow me to repeat the question: On what grounds did you state that this should have been a secret operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I didn't state that. I said that it could have been a secret operation. It might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But why might it have been a secret operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might have been because this was an illegal act of removing a large mass grave to another site. And in my view, this could be a reason for it to be a secret operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with that assignment of yours, from the 25th of August to the 5th of September, did you spend any time in the main staff in Crna Rijeka in connection with your activities?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
